Is Zapier worth it for a small business?

For simple hand-offs between two apps, often yes. For jobs with many steps or a check before sending, it is less clear.

Checked 2026-11-21. Menus in other products change, so a label may differ slightly on your screen.

Short answer: Zapier is worth it for a small office when the job is a simple hand-off between two apps that needs no judgement, such as "new form entry, add a row to the spreadsheet". It gets harder to justify when jobs have many steps, break often, or need someone to check the result before it goes out. Start with one small job on the free plan and see how it feels.

What Zapier does, in one paragraph

Zapier moves information from one app to another. You build a "Zap": an event that starts it (the trigger), then one or more things it does (the actions). If you want the longer story on how it feels to build, see Is Zapier hard to use? This page is about the other question: is it worth the money and effort for an office your size?

When Zapier is worth it

  • Simple hand-offs. A form is submitted and a row appears in a sheet. A payment arrives and a message goes to your team chat. A new customer is added in one tool and copied to another.
  • The same thing every time. If you could write the rule on a sticky note with no "it depends", Zapier will follow it.
  • Nobody needs to look first. If it is fine for the result to happen the moment the trigger fires, that is exactly what Zapier is for.
  • Popular apps on both ends. Ready-made connections and templates make these quick to set up.

For jobs like these, it can save real time each week. It is a solid, long-established product.

What it costs, and why the bill can grow

Zapier prices by "tasks", not by users. Per Zapier's help pages, a task is counted when an action step in a Zap completes successfully. Triggers, filters, paths, the Formatter tool and delays do not count, and neither do failed steps or test runs.

So one Zap run can use more than one task. If a Zap has a trigger and three actions, each run uses three tasks. Forty runs a month is 120 tasks. A job that runs every time an email arrives, or for every row in a big sheet, can add up much faster than you expect.

Plan names on zapier.com at the time of writing are Free, Professional, Team and Enterprise. The Free plan includes 100 tasks a month and only two-step Zaps (one trigger, one action). Multi-step Zaps need a paid plan. At the time of writing, Professional starts at $19.99 a month billed yearly, or $29.99 billed monthly, for 750 tasks. Zapier lists higher task tiers above that. Check the pricing page, because prices change.

If you go over your tasks, Zapier either stops your Zaps until the next cycle or, if you turn on pay-per-task, bills extra tasks at a higher rate. Read that setting before you switch it on.

Where small offices get stuck

  • Multi-step set-ups. Every extra step is another field to match, another test, and another task per run. A five-step Zap is a small project.
  • Fixing failures. When a step fails, Zapier records it in Zap history, and you can replay the failed run from there. Paid plans can also retry automatically after temporary problems. But working out why something failed, such as a renamed column or a changed field, usually falls to whoever built the Zap. If that person is you, it is one more thing on your list.
  • Work that needs judgement. "Send a reminder, but not to that customer, and not if we emailed last week" turns into filters and paths, each to be built and tested.
  • Review before it is sent. Zaps run on their own. Zapier does have a step, called Human in the Loop, that pauses a Zap until someone approves it. It needs a paid plan, and it is extra set-up.

None of this means Zapier is the wrong tool. It means the cost is partly money and partly your time keeping it running.

What to try first, if you are a beginner

  1. Check what your apps already do. QuickBooks, Outlook and your spreadsheet tool all have some built-in automation, and it costs nothing extra. See invoice reminders in QuickBooks Online, what Outlook can send automatically and what Smartsheet can send. Many Microsoft 365 business plans also include Power Automate for standard connectors such as Outlook, so an office on Microsoft 365 may already have a similar tool.
  2. Pick one small job. One trigger, one action, two popular apps, no judgement needed. Write it as: "When [this happens] in [app], do [that] in [other app]."
  3. Build it on the free plan. In Zapier you create a Zap, choose the trigger app and event, choose the action app and event, then match the fields. Test each step, then choose Publish. Zapier tests the action for real, so use a test record you do not mind creating.
  4. Watch it for a few weeks. Open Zap history now and then, and see how many tasks it uses.
  5. Decide with real numbers. If the free plan is enough, stay there. If you need more steps or tasks, you will know what you are paying for.

If you spend more time fixing a Zap than the job ever took by hand, that is a fair sign it is the wrong job for Zapier, not that you did something wrong.
